plan: [ This is strategically equivalent to a second‑price auction: the highest sealed bid wins and pays the second-highest bid. In such auctions, bidding one’s true value is a dominant strategy—it maximizes expected profit regardless of others’ strategies. Overbidding risks winning at a price above value; underbidding risks losing when winning would have yielded positive surplus. There is only 1 round and no history to learn from, so no adjustments are needed. Therefore, bid exactly my private value to ensure I win whenever price is below or equal to my value and avoid negative surplus. ]

[ This is strategically equivalent to a sealed-bid second-price auction because the winner pays the second-highest sealed bid. With independent private values, bidding your true value is a weakly dominant strategy: overbidding risks paying more than your value; underbidding risks losing profitable wins. There is no prior history to exploit and only one round, so maximize expected profit by setting the exit price equal to my value. My value is 18, so I bid 18. ]

[ With private, independent values and payment equal to the second-highest sealed bid, this mechanism is strategically equivalent to a second-price auction. The weakly dominant strategy is to bid truthfully. Overbidding risks winning at a price above my value; underbidding causes lost profitable wins without reducing expected price when winning. There’s only 1 round, so no learning/dynamics matter. I will bid my value exactly: 31. ]
